note.explanation: Intermolecular forces are attractions between molecules. Stronger attractions generally mean higher melting and boiling points. Polar molecules can attract by dipole-dipole forces, and hydrogen bonding is a particularly strong type of dipole-dipole attraction.
examples: HCl molecules attract because the H and Cl atoms have partial charges.
Water molecules form hydrogen bonds because water has highly polar O—H bonds.
note.checkAnswer: Hydrogen bonding; the O—H bonds in water are highly polar.
note.simple: Molecules can pull on other molecules. A stronger pull usually takes more heat to separate the molecules, so the substance has a higher boiling point.
note.checkQuestion: What type of intermolecular attraction occurs between water molecules?
note.title: Intermolecular Forces of Attraction
steps: Identify whether the molecules are polar.
For polar molecules, look for partial positive and partial negative charges that attract.
If hydrogen is covalently bonded to F, O or N, identify the attraction as hydrogen bonding.
Relate stronger intermolecular forces to higher melting or boiling points.
note.answer: Intermolecular forces are attractions between molecules. Dipole-dipole forces occur between polar molecules; hydrogen bonding is a strong special case involving hydrogen covalently bonded to F, O or N.

options: The H₂O molecules have strong hydrogen bonds between them.
The H₂O molecules have ionic bonds between them.
Water molecules have no attractive forces between them.
The covalent O—H bonds break when water boils.
mcqs.stem: Why does water have a relatively high boiling point compared with many small molecules?
rationales: Correct: strong hydrogen bonds between water molecules require considerable energy to overcome.
Incorrect: water consists of covalent molecules, not ions held together by ionic bonds.
Incorrect: water molecules do attract each other, particularly through hydrogen bonding.
Incorrect: boiling separates molecules by overcoming intermolecular attractions; it does not normally break the O—H covalent bonds.

mcqs.stem: What attraction occurs between the partially positive end of one HCl molecule and the partially negative end of another?
rationales: Correct: oppositely charged ends of polar molecules attract by dipole-dipole forces.
Incorrect: HCl molecules are not ions joined by ionic bonds.
Incorrect: HCl is not a metal and does not have metallic bonding.
Incorrect: covalent bonds join atoms within an HCl molecule, not separate HCl molecules.

mcqs.stem: In which molecule is hydrogen bonding expected between the molecules?
rationales: Correct: hydrogen is covalently bonded to highly electronegative fluorine, so hydrogen bonding can occur between HF molecules.
Incorrect: chlorine is not one of the elements F, O or N specified for hydrogen bonding in this section.
Incorrect: bromine is not one of the elements F, O or N specified for hydrogen bonding in this section.
Incorrect: iodine is not one of the elements F, O or N specified for hydrogen bonding in this section.

options: The same boiling point in every case
mcqs.stem: If the intermolecular forces between molecules of a liquid become stronger, what generally happens to its boiling point?
rationales: Correct: stronger attractions require more energy to overcome, so the boiling point is higher.
Incorrect: stronger attractions do not make it easier for molecules to separate.
Incorrect: a liquid has a boiling point under a given pressure.
Incorrect: boiling point depends on the strength of the intermolecular forces and is not always the same.

mcqs.stem: Among the three states of matter, where does this section say intermolecular forces are weakest?
rationales: Correct: the section states that these forces are weakest among molecules of gases.
Incorrect: the section places liquid molecules between gases and solids in relative force strength.
Incorrect: the section states that intermolecular forces are strongest among molecules of solids.
Incorrect: this option refers to bonding within molecules, not forces between molecules in the three states.

options: A larger difference in electronegativity makes the O—H bond highly polar.
Oxygen and hydrogen have equal electronegativity.
The water molecules are held together by ionic bonds.
The O—H covalent bonds are broken whenever water molecules attract.
mcqs.stem: Why do water molecules form strong hydrogen-bond attractions with one another?
rationales: Correct: the large electronegativity difference makes the O—H bonds highly polar, allowing strong attractions between molecules.
Incorrect: the section says the difference in electronegativity makes the O—H bond highly polar.
Incorrect: water consists of covalent molecules, not molecules joined to one another by ionic bonds.
Incorrect: hydrogen bonding is an attraction between molecules; it does not require breaking the O—H covalent bonds.

written.finalAnswer: They have weak intermolecular forces of attraction, so little energy is needed to separate their molecules.

written.text: Why HF is a liquid while HCl is a gas?
written.finalAnswer: HF molecules form hydrogen bonds because hydrogen is covalently bonded to highly electronegative fluorine. HCl molecules have dipole-dipole forces, which are weaker than hydrogen bonds, so HF has a higher boiling point and is a liquid while HCl is a gas.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen is covalently bonded to highly electronegative fluorine in HF, so HF molecules form hydrogen bonds.
HCl molecules attract each other by dipole-dipole forces.
Hydrogen bonds are stronger than the dipole-dipole forces between HCl molecules.
Therefore, HF has a higher boiling point and is a liquid while HCl is a gas.

written.text: Why does iodine exist as a solid while Cl₂ exist as a gas?
written.finalAnswer: I₂ molecules have stronger intermolecular forces of attraction than Cl₂ molecules, so more energy is needed to separate them. Thus iodine is a solid while Cl₂ is a gas.

examTips: This topic can appear as a short or constructed-response question asking you to explain a difference in boiling point or physical state, such as HF and HCl.

For a comparison, make the relative strength clear: stronger intermolecular forces generally give a higher boiling point and, for solids, a higher melting point.

steps.why: HCl is given in the section as an example of a polar compound.
Chlorine attracts the shared electron pair more strongly because its electronegativity is greater than hydrogen's.
steps.text: Chlorine attracts the shared pair of electrons more strongly than hydrogen.

steps.why: This unequal attraction makes the bond polar and gives the atoms partial charges.
steps.text: The bond becomes polar: Hδ⁺ × Clδ⁻.

steps.why: Opposite partial charges on neighbouring molecules attract one another.
steps.text: The partial charges cause neighbouring HCl molecules to attract by dipole-dipole forces.

example.question: Explain how HCl molecules attract each other by dipole-dipole forces.
example.answer: Chlorine attracts the shared electron pair more strongly than hydrogen, making HCl polar (Hδ⁺ × Clδ⁻). The partial charges cause neighbouring HCl molecules to attract by dipole-dipole forces.

explain.title: What are intermolecular forces?
explain.body: The forces of attraction which are present between the molecules of elements and compounds are named as intermolecular forces of attraction. These attractive forces are generally very weak as compared to the bonding forces present between the atoms of substances. Among the three states of matter, these forces are the weakest among the molecules of the gases and the strongest among the molecules of solids.

explain.title: Why their strength matters
explain.body: Intermolecular forces affect physical properties. The stronger the forces among the molecules of a liquid, the higher its boiling point; stronger intermolecular forces also give a solid a higher melting point.

explain.title: Dipole-dipole forces
explain.body: These attractive forces are present between the molecules of a polar compound like HCl. In HCl, chlorine attracts the shared pair of electrons more strongly than hydrogen, making the bond polar. The partial charges cause HCl molecules to attract each other; these are dipole-dipole forces.

explain.title: Hydrogen bonding
explain.body: Hydrogen bonding is a special case of dipole-dipole attractive forces. When hydrogen is covalent bonded to highly electronegative elements like F, O or N then the large difference of electronegativity values will make the covalent bond highly polar. Strong dipole-dipole attractions are then observed among the molecules. Water molecules form hydrogen bonds, helping explain water's relatively high melting and boiling points.

mistakes: Do not confuse intermolecular forces between molecules with covalent bonds within a molecule.
Do not call every dipole-dipole attraction hydrogen bonding; hydrogen bonding is the special case involving hydrogen bonded to F, O or N.
When explaining a higher boiling point, state that stronger intermolecular forces require more energy to overcome.
Do not say that boiling normally breaks the covalent bonds within the molecules.
